nameStory: The snowdrop gets its name from its pure white flowers that hang like tiny drops of snow from slender green stems. These charming flowers often peek through actual snow in late winter, creating the illusion of snow that has crystallized into perfect little bells. The scientific name 'nivalis' comes from the Latin word for snow, reinforcing this winter-white connection.
description: Common snowdrop is a small bulbous plant that stands just 3-6 inches tall, producing distinctive white bell-shaped flowers that dangle from thin stems. Each plant emerges from an underground bulb with narrow, strap-like leaves that have a blue-green color. The flowers hang singly from each stem like tiny white lanterns, each with six petals marked by green accents. This early spring bloomer often forms colonies that spread slowly over time, creating carpets of white flowers in favorable locations.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Single white bell-shaped flower hangs from each stem, with six petals that have distinctive green markings - look for a green 'V' or horseshoe shape on the outer petals

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Two to three narrow, strap-like leaves per bulb with a distinctive blue-green color and smooth, waxy texture that feels cool and slightly thick to the touch

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low-growing plant only 3-6 inches tall that often forms small colonies, with flowers that nod downward on thin, delicate stems

idTips.label: Bulbs
idTips.description: Small white bulbs about the size of a large marble, found 2-3 inches underground and often producing offsets that create clusters

habitat: In New England, snowdrops are typically found in cultivated areas like gardens, old home sites, and cemetery grounds where they've escaped or been naturalized. They prefer partially shaded spots with moist, well-drained soil and are often found under deciduous trees or along woodland edges. Look for them near old foundations, stone walls, or abandoned homesteads where they may persist long after gardens have been forgotten.

seasonality.spring: Flowers appear in late February through March, often pushing through snow. The distinctive white bells with green markings are unmistakable during this early bloom period when few other flowers are present.
seasonality.summer: Leaves persist until early summer, then die back completely as the plant goes dormant. By midsummer, no trace of the plant remains above ground.
seasonality.fall: Plants are completely dormant with no visible growth above ground. The bulbs are developing energy underground for next year's bloom.
seasonality.winter: No above-ground growth is visible until very late winter, when flower buds may begin emerging through snow and frozen ground in warm spells.

funFact: Snowdrops actually generate their own heat through a process called thermogenesis, which helps them melt through snow and frozen ground to emerge in late winter - they can raise their internal temperature up to 18°F above the surrounding air temperature!
confusionNotes: Don't confuse snowdrops with snowflakes (Leucojum species), which have similar white flowers but are larger overall and have equal-sized petals all marked with green spots rather than the snowdrop's distinctive green 'V' marking on outer petals only. Memory trick: snowdrops 'drop' down on unequal petals, snowflakes have uniform petals like real snowflakes have equal sides.
contextualKnowledge: Common snowdrop is not native to New England but has been cultivated here since colonial times and occasionally naturalizes in suitable habitats. These plants are sometimes called 'fair maids of February' in old garden literature, though in our colder New England climate they typically bloom in March.
compareHints: Common snowdrop is smaller and more delicate than its relatives greater snowdrop and green snowdrop, both of which are taller and less commonly encountered in New England. Greater snowdrop has larger flowers and broader leaves, while green snowdrop has distinctive yellow-green leaf markings rather than the pure blue-green of common snowdrop. Common snowdrop remains the most widespread and garden-worthy species in our region.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Greater snowdrop is larger and more robust than common snowdrop (Galanthus nivalis) in all aspects - taller stems, broader leaves, and bigger flowers.
Green snowdrop differs from common snowdrop by having broader, blue-green leaves and a single green mark on the inner petals rather than two.
